title: [Chapitre] VI. Analysis situs (deuxième mouture) : notes manuscrites (18-20/06/1986).

deep.reconstruction:
Context: in the second draft of 'Analysis situs' (1986) Grothendieck is building tame or piecewise-linear topology combinatorially. The basic object is a set 𝔉 of 'figures', e.g. finite cell or simplicial complexes inside a fixed ambient space. 𝔉 carries several relations:
- G ≤ F: G is a subfigure (subcomplex) of F.
- G ≼ F: G is a subdivision or refinement of F with the same support.
- G ≪ F: the 'précéder' relation. Geometrically the support of G lies in the support of F, i.e. G is a subfigure of some subdivision of F.
- F ∥ G: disjointness.
- F ≬ G: compatibility. Geometrically, F and G are both subfigures of a common figure ({F,G} has an upper bound for ≤).

The previous page showed what determines what:
- Either of ≤ and ≪ determines ∥ (1.24).
- ≪ determines ≼ (1.25): F ≼ G iff F ≪ G and F, G are disjoint from the same figures, i.e. same support.
- ≪ determines the set 𝓛 of 'points' as the minimal nonempty elements (1.26).
- ≪ together with ≬ determines ≤ (1.27): G ≤ F iff G ≪ F and G ≬ F. This is correct: if G and F are both subfigures of some H and |G| ⊂ |F|, then G is a subcomplex of F.

This page draws the conclusion (1.28). The 'structure' on 𝔉 (the transcription's 'I' is very probably 𝔉) can be specified by any of three pairs of primitive relations:
1. (≤, ≪), boxed as the chosen option.
2. (≤, ≼). A margin note next to it says 'No, that doesn't suffice, according to the new point of view'.
3. (≪, ≬).

In the first draft he took (≤, ≼) as primitive and defined ≪ (1.29) as the relation generated by them: G ≪ F iff there is F' with G ≤ F' ≼ F. This matches the intuitive geometric criterion based on subdivision rather than refinement.

The technical difficulty: proving transitivity of the generated relation needs an exchange axiom. If F' ≼ F ≤ H, one must find H' ≼ H with F' ≤ H', i.e. a subdivision of a subcomplex extends to a subdivision of the whole complex. Proving the order properties in general needs further 'somewhat ad hoc' conditions.

He therefore switches to (≤, ≪) as primitive, which he finds technically simplest. A diagonal margin note, added later, records the change of rules from p. 20 on: ≼ is now defined from ≤ and ≪, not ≪ from ≤ and ≼. He calls the (≪, ≬) presentation a mere curiosity.

The next page fixes the axiom set: two partial orders ≤ and ≪ on 𝔉 with F ≤ G ⇒ F ≪ G. From these he recovers the points and the embedding of 𝔉 into the power set of the set 𝓜 defined there by (1.20).
errors: He says it was hard to derive 'réflexivité' for ≪. A relation generated by the reflexive relations ≤ and ≼ is automatically reflexive, so the property that is actually hard must be antisymmetry. Transitivity also needs a subdivision-extension (exchange) axiom. Probably a slip of the pen.

The margin note 'ça ne suffit pas' sits next to option (≤, ≼). It contradicts the main text, which says the first draft worked with (≤, ≼). It reflects a later change of viewpoint, not a mathematical error on the page itself.
Whether (≤, ≼) really fails to determine ≪ under the new axioms is asserted but not shown.

ideas.what: Axiomatize a category of polyhedral or tame 'figures' as a set with two compatible partial orders: subfigure ≤ and support-inclusion ≪, with ≤ ⊂ ≪. Derived from these: disjointness, refinement, points, and compatibility.
ideas.modern_name: Order-theoretic or point-free axiomatization of PL / tame topology (cf. o-minimal structures, abstract cell complexes)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Tame topology programme of the Esquisse (Grothendieck 1984), o-minimality (van den Dries, Pillay–Steinhorn, Knight); abstract cell complexes (Kovalevsky); no standard credit for this two-order formulation
ideas.where_published: Only the general wish for a 'topologie modérée' appears in Esquisse d'un programme §5; the axiomatic details are unpublished.

ideas.what: Interdefinability analysis: (≤, ≪), (≤, ≼) and (≪, ≬) as alternative primitive pairs, using G ≤ F ⇔ G ≪ F ∧ G ≬ F and F ≼ G ⇔ F ≪ G ∧ same disjointness behaviour.
ideas.modern_name: Choice of primitive relations (definitional equivalence) in a poset-based theory

ideas.what: Defining ≪ as the relation generated by subcomplex and subdivision, which requires a subdivision-extension (exchange) property for transitivity.
ideas.modern_name: Extension of subdivisions from subcomplexes; composition of relations up to cofinal refinement

missed.claim: An abstract, point-free axiomatics of tame figures, starting from two partial orders (≤, ≪) on the set of figures and reconstructing points, disjointness and subdivision. It is a concrete attempt at the 'topologie modérée' of the Esquisse that was never published or developed.
missed.quote: il semblerait que ce soit de partir de ≤, ≪ qui soit le plus simple. C'est l'approche que je vais suivre tantôt.
missed.why_it_might_matter_today: It offers a possible order-theoretic foundation for o-minimal or PL geometry, comparable to locale-theoretic point-free topology. On this page it is only the choice of primitives; substance would depend on the axioms worked out on later pages.

deep.surprise_reason: The page is a methodological remark choosing which primitive relations to axiomatize. It is of historical interest as a record of Grothendieck's unpublished tame-topology foundations, but it contains no new theorem.
transcription_corrections: Line 2: the final symbol is likely 𝔉 (script F), not 'I'. The word before it is unclear ('d'étalée' is doubtful).
Third option in (1.28): the symbol is ≬ ('between', the compatibility relation used in (1.27) on the previous page), not '≴'. It is written (≪, ≬).
The margin note reads roughly 'Non, ça ne suffit pas, d'après nouveau point de vue pris en vue…' and is attached to option (≤, ≼).
The diagonal margin note is a later addition: 'J'ai changé la règle du jeu (1.29) depuis p. 20, et ne considère plus que ≪ soit défini par ≤, ≼ mais plutôt que ≼ soit défini par ≤, ≪'.
Of the two transcription variants 'géométrique' / '[intuitif]', 'intuitif' seems to be the main reading and 'géométrique' an insertion. The struck word ('conceptuel'?) is illegible.
The main text has 'de réflexivité', likely intended as antisymmetry; the transcription is faithful to what is written.
